chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Zurara, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon them), who said:

When Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) married his mother to his slave, and he himself married his female slave, Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan sent him a letter blaming him, saying: 'You have lowered your nobility and your lineage.'

So Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) wrote back to him: 'Indeed, Allah the Exalted raised every humble thing through Islam, perfected the deficient, and removed blame through it; so there is no blame upon a Muslim, and indeed, blame is the blame of ignorance.'
As for my marrying my mother, I only intended thereby to show her kindness/piety.'
When the letter reached Abd al-Malik, he said: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn has done two things that no one else does; for indeed, by that, he has increased in nobility.'

key_terms.عَبْدُ الْمَلِكِ بْنُ مَرْوَانَ: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, the Umayyad Caliph

ai.seo_question: What was the reason for Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn's marriage of his mother to her slave?
ai.summary: This hadith from the chapter on marital compatibility (Kafa'ah) illustrates how Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS) challenged the Umayyad aristocratic notion that nobility is strictly genealogical by marrying his mother to her former slave. His concise reply to Caliph Abd al-Malik emphasizes that Islam purifies social hierarchies, rendering pre-Islamic notions of 'blame' obsolete for those acting in piety. The Caliph’s subsequent acknowledgment that this act increased the Imam's status highlights the Shia theological principle that spiritual merit and divine elevation supersede political or tribal lineage.
